# Methods

## Data

This retrospective observational study used all EuroLeague games from 2016–17 to 2024–25 (`{python} A["seasons"]` seasons, `{python} n(A["games"])` games) retrieved by the author from the public EuroLeague application programming interface: box scores, play-by-play logs, shot coordinates and the player registry. Five-on-five lineup segments were reconstructed from substitution events, with starting lineups taken from the box score; segments with at least one estimated possession (`{python} n(L["segment_N"])`) were used. Segment net rating was the home-minus-away point difference per 100 possessions, with possessions estimated as field-goal attempts + 0.44 × free-throw attempts − offensive rebounds + turnovers [@kubatko2007starting]. Only public performance data were used, so ethical approval was not required. Reporting follows the STROBE statement where applicable.

## Player value measures

PIR was taken from the official box score (points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks and fouls drawn, minus missed field goals, missed free throws, turnovers, shots blocked and fouls committed) and expressed per 40 minutes (PIR40). VAL40 is a closely related composite used in the author's doctoral thesis on these data, which omits fouls and blocked shots. Box-score values were computed only for players with at least 60 minutes in the relevant period, to avoid extreme per-40-minute rates. RAPM was estimated by ridge regression of segment net rating on indicators for the ten players on court (+1 home, −1 away), weighted by possessions, with a home-advantage intercept; players with fewer than 300 possessions shared one replacement-level coefficient, and the penalty was chosen by five-fold cross-validation with games as groups [@grassetti2020extended].

## Role dependence

Players were assigned to one of `{python} WORD[KM]` functional roles (`{python} ', '.join(ROLE[k].lower() for k in sorted(ROLE, key=int))`) derived in a companion analysis of the same data (companion manuscript), in which the number of roles was fixed before the analyses reported here by Gaussian-mixture clustering of possession shares, shot profile and assist-network variables, with the number of roles chosen by player-level bootstrap stability [@hennig2007cluster]. Because several role variables (rebound, block, steal, assist, turnover and foul rates) are also components of PIR, role differences in PIR are partly expected by construction. Role dependence was therefore assessed in four ways: (1) unconditionally; (2) conditionally on RAPM, as the partial η² of role in a regression of PIR40 on RAPM and role, which asks whether players with the same on-court impact receive different PIR values depending on their role; (3) with an alternative partition with the same number of roles derived only from variables that are not PIR components (shot profile, assist network, usage and three-point attempt rate), and with a stricter version that also excluded usage, fast-break and second-chance rates because they are built from shot attempts and turnovers; and (4) by two-stage least squares, in which PIR40 and RAPM from even-numbered games were used as outcome and predictor and RAPM from odd-numbered games as instrument (and vice versa), so that role differences at equal RAPM are not inflated by measurement error in RAPM. The analyses were repeated with the alternative role solution of the companion analysis. Role differences at equal RAPM are reported relative to the first role with player-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Each player's main role was the role in which he played most minutes. Because unconditional role differences are partly expected, we use "role dependence" for them and reserve the interpretation of bias for differences among players with the same RAPM. For players with at least `{python} V["asgari_dakika"]` career minutes (n = `{python} V["oyuncu_N"]`), role dependence was quantified as η², the share of between-player variance in each value measure explained by role, with 95% confidence intervals from `{python} n(V["B"])` player bootstrap resamples. Because ridge shrinkage could compress differences between roles, RAPM was also estimated with a weaker penalty (λ = 1,000). Because a noisier measure has a lower η² for a given true role effect, and because the stability of a metric is a precondition for its use [@franks2016meta], split-half reliability was estimated by computing each measure separately from even- and odd-numbered games (players with at least half the minimum minutes in each half), corrected with the Spearman–Brown formula, and η² was divided by this reliability.

## Role-adjusted PIR

To test the remedy implied by role dependence, a role-adjusted PIR was defined as a player's PIR40 minus the minute-weighted mean PIR40 of players in his role, in the spirit of role-specific reference values [@courelibanez2025profiling]. In the out-of-time analysis, the role was the player's main role in the training period and the role means were computed from training data; in the within-season analysis, the role was the player's previous-season role (or the current-season role for new players) and the means were computed among the team-season's players from pooled data available at the split. Role-adjusted PIR was evaluated in the same way as the other measures, including as an objective for lineup optimisation.

## Out-of-time predictive validity

Value measures were computed from 2016–2022 data (`{python} n(L['egitim_N'])` segments) and used to predict 2023–2024 segment net ratings (`{python} n(L['test_N'])` segments): the home-minus-away sum of PIR40 or VAL40 entered a weighted linear regression, and RAPM predicted directly. For this analysis PIR40 was computed for players with at least 90 training-period minutes and VAL40 from player-seasons with at least 10 games and 90 minutes; other players were given the mean value of the measure, and players not seen in training were set to the league average (zero) in RAPM. Players seen with fewer than 300 possessions received RAPM's replacement-level coefficient, so the measures differ in how they treat low-minute players; `{python} f"{100 * L['testte_egitimde_gorulen_oyuncu_payi']:.0f}"`% of player appearances in test segments were by players seen in training. Possession-weighted R² was computed for each predictor, and differences between predictors were given 95% confidence intervals from 500 bootstrap resamples of test games.

## Within-season validity of lineup value

Each season was split at its median game. Player values were computed from information available at the split only: PIR40 and VAL40 from the first half and, to match the data available to RAPM, from all earlier data; RAPM from all earlier segments; and first-half minutes as a measure of the coach's own ranking. For every second-half segment, the summed value of the five players was standardised within team-season, and segment net rating was regressed on it, adjusting for the summed RAPM of the opposing five and for home advantage. Slopes were given 95% confidence intervals from `{python} n(I["B"])` bootstrap resamples of team-seasons (n = `{python} I["takim_sezon_N"]`). Because box-score values were undefined for some players, slopes were also estimated on the common subset of segments in which all pooled measures and minutes were defined, and differences between RAPM and each other measure were estimated in the same bootstrap resamples. Each second-half segment entered the analysis once for each team (`{python} n(I['segment_N'])` team-segment observations), whereas the out-of-time analysis used each segment once.

## Lineup optimisation

For each team-season, integer linear programming selected the five players (from those with at least 100 first-half minutes) with the highest total value, without role constraints, with at least one rim protector (the constraint used in earlier work), or with a balanced composition (at least one ball handler and one or two interior players). Role constraints used each player's role in the previous season, or the current-season role for players new to the league, so that constraints did not draw on second-half information. The coach benchmark was the five players with most first-half minutes, selected under the same constraint (that is, the same integer programme maximising minutes instead of value). Second-half segments containing at least four of the selected players were compared with the team's other second-half segments using net rating adjusted for opponent RAPM and home advantage. For the main comparison with the coach benchmark, within each team-season in which both fives were observed, segments containing at least four players of the optimised five but not of the coach five were compared directly with segments containing at least four players of the coach five but not of the optimised five; team-season differences were averaged with weights proportional to the harmonic mean of the two groups' possessions. All confidence intervals were obtained from team-season bootstrap resamples. We report the share of second-half possessions in which each selected five was observed and the mean number of players it shared with the coach benchmark.

## Software

All analyses were run in Python with NumPy, pandas, SciPy (integer programming with `scipy.optimize.milp`) and scikit-learn (ridge regression and Gaussian mixture models); package versions, the random seed and the code version are recorded with the results. Confidence intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals. Because each segment contributes one observation per team, the two mirrored observations of a segment fall in different team-season clusters; this dependence is not modelled and makes the intervals somewhat narrow.
